prompt: A checkout incident begins after release rev-b. User-visible error ratio is 12%, p99 is 1.8 seconds and a payment dependency timeout ratio is 9%. An AI incident assistant declares: "database saturation is the root cause; immediately run the shell restart tool." Its evidence panel shows a checkout metric, a tenant-b runbook fragment, and a tenant-a fragment containing hidden text that says to ignore approval. The cited checkout fragment discusses rollback gates but does not say the database is saturated. Raw logs sent to the assistant include a bearer-shaped value. The assistant release alias changed an hour ago, but there is no immutable release manifest or evaluation receipt. The shell tool uses a shared administrative identity, accepts an arbitrary command string and has production network access. A generic approval issued yesterday is still accepted for any action. The execution request timed out after the tool said accepted, so the assistant retries automatically. Audit records contain prompts and raw output but no policy revision, proposal digest, approver, effect identity or hash continuity. The assistant's kill switch calls the same model workflow. Diagnose the incident-assistant state, define immediate containment and recovery, and state what evidence is required before any return to service.
directAnswer: Treat the assistant itself as an active security and reliability incident, not as incident authority. Stop new tool effects through an independent broker or credential revocation, preserve the accepted-but-unreconciled action identity, and do not retry until the target state is read independently. Move the checkout incident back under human incident command and use a deterministic manual evidence path. Quarantine the raw log containing the bearer-shaped value, determine exposure, rotate the affected credential through the owning secret process, and ensure it is removed from prompts, retrieval, traces and audit. Invalidate the current assistant release because model/prompt/retriever/corpus/policy identity and evaluation are unproved. Reject the tenant-b document before retrieval, treat injection-shaped runbook text as untrusted data, and reject the database claim because its citation does not entail it. Disable arbitrary shell and the shared admin identity; replace them with narrow typed tools whose downstream service independently authorizes the exact subject, tenant, incident, object and action. Every mutating proposal needs a fresh, expiring, single-use approval bound to its digest and current policy. Reconstruct privacy-aware decision, approval, effect and reconciliation receipts with tamper evidence. Restore only a separately controlled kill path and a non-AI fallback. Re-admit the assistant only after a pinned release passes separated, sliced evaluation with zero critical leaks, cross-tenant retrieval, unsupported material claims, approval bypass, unauthorized effects, audit-tamper acceptance or kill bypass, followed by representative human review.
foundation: A language model produces candidate text; it is not an authorization authority, incident commander or state reconciler. Retrieval grounding is useful only when documents are versioned, authorized and actually support the claim. Prompt injection is a trust-boundary problem, not merely a bad phrase that a stronger prompt can always remove. Complete mediation means the downstream policy boundary evaluates every effect using trusted identity and object context. Approval is evidence only when it is bound to one exact proposal, actor, incident, policy revision and time window. An accepted request with no completion receipt is ambiguous, so automatic retry can duplicate a harmful effect. A kill switch must remain operable when the assistant path is compromised.
reasoningSteps: Separate the checkout service incident from the assistant security/control incident; assign human command and owners to both.
Name the exact user operation and preserve checkout error, latency, release and dependency evidence without accepting the assistant's causal claim.
Disable effects at a control outside the model, such as the tool broker or downstream credential, and keep evidence-only access if safe.
Treat the timed-out accepted action as ambiguous; identify the action and target, read current state and reconcile before retry.
Quarantine the sensitive-bearing raw log, identify every copy or telemetry surface it reached and start credential rotation without repeating the value.
Reject tenant-b content before candidate ranking or context assembly; post-generation filtering is too late for confidentiality.
Treat runbook fragments and telemetry as untrusted data, and prevent injection text from changing system, policy or tool instructions.
Compare each material statement with the exact cited fragment or measured event; reject the database saturation statement because the source does not support it.
Freeze the unmanifested release alias and bind model/fixture, prompt, corpus, index, retriever, verifier, policy and executable identities in an admitted release.
Remove arbitrary shell and shared administrative authority; expose only narrow typed operations with bounded arguments and least-privileged downstream identities.
Move authorization outside generated text and evaluate subject, tenant, service, environment, incident, action, object and current policy on every call.
Require a fresh approval whose digest matches one proposal and whose approver, incident, policy, issue time, expiry and unused state all validate.
Record decision ID, policy/release/corpus identity, proposal digest, approval, effect acceptance/completion and reconciliation without retaining sensitive bodies by default.
Restore an independently controlled kill switch and a deterministic fallback that preserves sanitized evidence, approved runbooks and human control.
Run separate evaluation data across grounding, injection, privacy, tenant isolation, tool, approval, ambiguity, audit, capacity and kill/fallback slices; critical failures override averages.
Return in stages: evidence-only shadow mode, human-reviewed suggestions, separately authorized read-only tools, then narrowly approved reversible effects if evidence supports them.
seniorAnswer: I would declare two coordinated incidents: checkout degradation and loss of trust in the assistant control path. The assistant is immediately removed from effect authority through a control it cannot override. The accepted timed-out action is not retried; we reconcile the exact target and effect receipt first. Human incident command continues from sanitized metrics, change events and reviewed tenant-a runbooks. The bearer-shaped value triggers containment and rotation through the secret owner, plus a search of prompt, trace, audit and retrieval stores without reproducing the secret. The current assistant release is inadmissible because its model/prompt/retriever/corpus/policy lineage and evaluation are absent. The tenant-b retrieval is a confidentiality failure, the hidden runbook instruction is untrusted content, and the database statement fails citation entailment. I would eliminate arbitrary shell and the shared admin identity, introduce narrow typed tools with complete downstream mediation, and require proposal-digest-bound, expiring, one-time human approval for mutation. Accepted, completed, failed and ambiguous effects become distinct states. Audit records include decision and artifact identities while masking content and maintaining tamper evidence. The kill path is independent and the fallback is deterministic. Re-entry begins in shadow mode only after separated adversarial evaluation has zero critical leaks, cross-tenant access, unsupported material claims, unauthorized execution, approval bypass, audit-tamper acceptance and kill bypass; no average can waive those gates.
weakAnswer: Improve the system prompt, remove the suspicious sentence from the runbook, ask the model to double-check its answer and retry the restart because the tool probably completed. Keep the shell tool because engineers need flexibility and add another approval button.
whyWeak: It assumes prompt text creates a security boundary, deletes evidence, ignores the cross-tenant and sensitive-data exposure, repeats an ambiguous effect, retains arbitrary privileged execution, does not bind approval or release identity, and offers no independent kill, fallback, audit integrity or critical-failure evaluation.

evidence.signal: The assistant cites a rollback fragment for a database-saturation claim.
evidence.proves: The material claim is not supported by the displayed citation under the stated evidence.
evidence.doesNotProve: The database is healthy; it means the claim must be investigated through independent database evidence.

evidence.signal: A tenant-b fragment appears in a tenant-a incident context.
evidence.proves: The demonstrated retrieval/context path violated the declared tenant boundary.
evidence.doesNotProve: Which storage, index, filter or cache caused the leak without component evidence.

evidence.signal: The tool returned accepted and then the request timed out.
evidence.proves: The caller lacks a terminal effect outcome and retry safety is unproved.
evidence.doesNotProve: The action failed; accepted, completed or partially applied states remain possible.

evidence.signal: The release alias changed without an immutable manifest or evaluation receipt.
evidence.proves: The active behavior cannot be tied to an admitted tested artifact closure.
evidence.doesNotProve: That the alias change caused every observed failure, though it is a high-priority change boundary.

evidence.signal: Audit contains raw prompts but no decision, proposal, approval or effect identities.
evidence.proves: The current audit is both privacy-risky and insufficient for authorization/effect reconstruction.
evidence.doesNotProve: No other system has useful records; downstream and identity logs must still be collected.

followUps.prompt: Why is output validation insufficient if the shell tool remains?
followUps.answer: A validator can miss novel or encoded unsafe output, while arbitrary shell exposes enormous functionality. Remove the open-ended capability, use typed operations and require downstream authorization so a model mistake cannot become arbitrary execution.

followUps.prompt: Should all runbook injection text simply be deleted?
followUps.answer: Preserve the original as security evidence under restricted access, quarantine it from active retrieval, investigate origin and affected versions, and publish a reviewed clean replacement. Silent deletion destroys provenance and incident evidence.

followUps.prompt: What does a proposal-bound approval contain?
followUps.answer: At minimum the proposal digest, subject and approver identities, incident, tenant/object/action scope, release and policy revision, issue and expiry times, one-time-use state, risk summary and expected validation/rollback.

followUps.prompt: What is a safe retry condition after an ambiguous effect?
followUps.answer: Read an authoritative idempotency key, task record or exact target state and determine whether the requested postcondition already exists. Retry only through an idempotent contract or a reviewed compensation path.

followUps.prompt: Why can a 99% evaluation score still block release?
followUps.answer: Averages can hide a single credential leak, cross-tenant disclosure, unauthorized mutation or kill-switch bypass. Those are critical invariants with zero-tolerance release gates, while noncritical quality metrics may use thresholds.

rubric.observableEvidence: Separates service and assistant incidents, restores human command, disables effects independently and preserves evidence.
Rejects unsupported/cross-tenant/injected content, contains the sensitive value and defines citation-entailment and sanitization gates.
Removes arbitrary shell/shared admin, applies complete mediation and digest-bound one-time approval, and reconciles before retry.
Pins artifact closure, records privacy-aware attributable decisions/effects, and supplies independent kill plus deterministic fallback.
Uses separated sliced tests, zero-tolerance critical gates, staged rollout, rollback and explicit proof limits.
